common_name: Snake Ceropegia (Zulu Bonnet)

planting.note: Grow in fast-draining, gritty cactus mix in a hanging basket or on a small trellis where the sprawling stems can scramble or trail; allow the mix to dry fully between waterings.

directions: Native to the Eastern Cape of South Africa, this collector succulent produces thick, gray-green, mottled stems patterned like snakeskin that sprawl along the ground or scramble and trail from a hanging container. Unlike the fine, wiry stems of string of hearts, its stems are stout and fleshy, storing water for long dry spells, and arise from a tuberous rootstock that should never sit in soggy mix. In summer, unusual maroon-and-cream stapeliad-like flowers with fused, hairy tips emerge along the stems, temporarily trapping small fly pollinators. Give it bright indirect light, sharp drainage, and water only once the mix is bone dry, especially through winter dormancy.
sources: Cactus and Succulent Society of America reference

common_name: Hearts Entangled

planting.note: Provide a small trellis, hoop, or hanging basket for the twining stems, and grow in fast-draining, gritty succulent mix that is allowed to dry between waterings.

directions: A South African twining succulent vine grown from a small tuber, valued by collectors for its slender wiry stems, sparse fleshy leaves, and remarkable flowers borne on long peduncles. Each bloom flares into a dark, bulbous, fringed hood fringed with fine purple-black hairs that briefly traps visiting flies, a pollination trick shared with its relatives sandersonii and woodii. Let the twining stems climb a small support or trail from a hanging pot, and water sparingly, allowing the gritty mix to dry out fully between soakings to avoid rotting the tuber. Bright indirect light and a warm, frost-free position keep it actively growing through the warm season before it rests in winter.
sources: Cactus and Succulent Society of America reference

common_name: Netted Chin Cactus (Spider Cactus)

planting.note: Plant offsets or nursery starts in spring into very well-drained, gritty mineral soil in bright light with a little midday shade; the sparse, curved spines lie close against the ribs, so avoid crowding that traps moisture against the body.

directions: Grow in a shallow pot of gritty, fast-draining cactus mix in bright light with shade from the harshest afternoon sun, watering only after the soil has dried completely. The flattened, glossy dark-green globe has broad, rounded ribs divided into chin-like humps, with a handful of slender, downward-curving spines pressed flat against the body in a net-like pattern. Native to rocky grassland in Rio Grande do Sul, Brazil and neighboring Uruguay, it produces large white to pale pink funnel-shaped flowers with a reddish throat from the crown in late spring. Keep dry and cool through winter dormancy and resume watering as new growth appears in spring.
sources: Cactus and Succulent Society of America

common_name: Monville's Chin Cactus

planting.note: Set out offsets or nursery starts in spring in mineral, gritty cactus mix and full sun to light shade; this is one of the larger-growing chin cacti and appreciates a deeper pot than most Gymnocalycium.

directions: Plant in gritty, mineral-rich cactus soil in full sun to very light shade, letting the mix dry fully between waterings. The solid gray-green to blue-green globe carries broad, low ribs with stout, outward-curving gray spines, and can eventually grow into a large, single-headed barrel. Native to rocky slopes in Córdoba Province, Argentina, it bears wide, funnel-shaped white to pale pink flowers up to several inches across from the crown in late spring and early summer. Provide a dry, cool winter rest to encourage strong flowering the following season.
sources: Cactus and Succulent Society of America
San Diego Cactus and Succulent Society

common_name: Spegazzini's Chin Cactus

planting.note: Plant in spring in very gritty, fast-draining mineral soil in full sun; native to high-altitude sites in the Andes foothills, it tolerates cooler nights and brief light frost better than most chin cacti as long as it stays dry.

directions: Grow in full sun in very gritty, mineral cactus mix, watering only after the soil has dried out completely. The flattened, blue-gray body has broad ribs formed into pronounced chin-like humps beneath each stout, curved gray-brown spine cluster, giving the plant a sculptural, banded look. Native to high-elevation rocky terrain near Salta, Argentina, it is among the more cold-tolerant Gymnocalycium species and produces large white to pale pink flowers with a red throat near the crown in early summer. Keep bone-dry and give maximum light through a cool winter rest.
sources: Cactus and Succulent Society of America

common_name: Cerro Prieto Pincushion Cactus

planting.note: Grow as a houseplant or xeriscape container plant in bright, filtered light in fast-draining cactus mix; this species exudes a milky sap when cut, so handle offsets carefully when dividing.

directions: Grow in bright, filtered light to partial sun in gritty, fast-draining cactus mix, watering only once the soil has dried fully. The pale gray-green globose stems cluster readily from the base and are covered in short, fine white spines with a few slender central spines, and unlike most Mammillaria the stem exudes a milky white latex when injured. Native to rocky hillsides in Guerrero and Oaxaca, Mexico, it produces creamy white to pale yellow flowers with a faint musky scent that open in the evening in summer. Give a cool, dry winter rest and separate rooted offsets in spring to propagate.
sources: Cactus and Succulent Society of America

common_name: Schiede's Pincushion Cactus

planting.note: Grow as a houseplant or xeriscape container plant in bright, filtered light in very gritty cactus mix; the dense golden spination needs strong light to stay tight and colorful.

directions: Plant in bright, filtered light to partial sun in fast-draining, mineral-rich cactus mix, letting the soil dry completely between waterings. Small, rounded stems are densely covered in fine, golden-yellow spines that nearly obscure the stem surface, and the plant offsets steadily to form a low, spreading cluster. Native to limestone outcrops in Hidalgo, Mexico, it bears small, pale pink to nearly white flowers ringing the crown in spring. Provide a dry, cool winter rest and divide offsets to propagate new plants.
sources: Cactus and Succulent Society of America
San Diego Cactus and Succulent Society

common_name: Wild's Pincushion Cactus

planting.note: Grow in a hanging basket or shallow pot in bright, filtered light in fast-draining cactus mix; the sprawling, freely branching stems are better suited to a wide container than a deep one.

directions: Grow in bright, filtered light to partial sun in gritty, fast-draining cactus mix, watering only after the soil has dried out fully. Slender, elongating stems branch and sprawl readily, eventually cascading over the pot's edge, and are set with fine white radial spines and a few slender hooked central spines. Native to rocky hillsides in Hidalgo and Querétaro, Mexico, it produces small white to pale pink flowers with a greenish throat clustered near the growing tips in spring and summer, followed by slender red seed pods. Give a cool, dry winter rest and trim or root stem cuttings to control size and propagate.
sources: Cactus and Succulent Society of America

common_name: Many-Nippled Pincushion Cactus

planting.note: Grow as a houseplant or xeriscape container plant in full sun to bright filtered light in mineral cactus mix; this species elongates into a columnar shape with age and eventually benefits from a deeper pot.

directions: Grow in full sun to bright filtered light in gritty, fast-draining cactus mix, watering only once the soil has dried completely. The dark green stem is densely packed with conical tubercles and sparse, short spines, and elongates into a columnar form over time, occasionally branching from the base with age. Native to rocky slopes in San Luis Potosí and Hidalgo, Mexico, it bears a ring of small pale pink to purplish flowers near the crown in spring. Provide a cool, dry winter rest and repot as the stem lengthens to keep it from toppling.
sources: Cactus and Succulent Society of America

common_name: Golden Sun Pincushion Cactus

planting.note: Grow as a houseplant or xeriscape container plant in full sun in very gritty cactus mix; strong direct light keeps the fine radiating spines bright golden-yellow and tightly packed.

directions: Plant in full sun in fast-draining, mineral cactus mix, letting the soil dry out completely between waterings. Small, clustering stems are covered in numerous fine, golden-yellow spines that radiate outward in a sunburst pattern from each areole, nearly hiding the stem beneath. Native to rocky outcrops in Querétaro, Mexico, it produces small, pale yellow to cream flowers near the crown in spring. Provide a cool, dry winter rest and separate offsets in spring to propagate new plants.
sources: Cactus and Succulent Society of America
San Diego Cactus and Succulent Society

common_name: Emerald Pink Moss Phlox (Hot-Pink Creeping Phlox)

planting.note: Plant in well-drained to dry, lean, neutral to slightly alkaline soil in full sun; Emerald Pink establishes quickly from container divisions set out in early spring and knits into a solid mat within a season or two.

directions: Plant in well-drained to dry, lean, neutral to slightly alkaline soil in full sun. Emerald Pink smothers its dark green, needle-like evergreen foliage each spring under a dense blanket of hot, saturated pink star-shaped flowers, a warmer and more vivid pink than the softer rose of 'Purple Beauty' or the blue-lavender of 'Emerald Blue'. The tight, fast-spreading mat knits into a weed-suppressing evergreen carpet well suited to rock gardens, slopes, and cascading over walls. Shear lightly right after bloom to keep the mat dense and compact, and avoid rich or poorly drained soil, which favors floppy growth and crown rot.

common_name: White Delight Moss Phlox (Pure White Creeping Phlox)

planting.note: Plant in well-drained to dry, lean, neutral to slightly alkaline soil in full sun; give White Delight sharp drainage from the start, since a pure-white cultivar shows soil splash and foliage decline from soggy crowns more readily than darker-flowered types.

directions: Plant in well-drained to dry, lean, neutral to slightly alkaline soil in full sun. White Delight covers its needle-like, dark green evergreen foliage in an unusually heavy flush of large, pure-white flowers each spring, giving a brighter, cleaner white than the faintly blushed blooms of 'Snowflake'. The dense, mat-forming habit makes it a strong companion planted alongside pink, red, or blue moss phlox cultivars to sharpen color contrast in a rock garden or slope planting. Shear lightly after flowering to maintain a tight cushion, and keep the crown on the dry side, since standing moisture is the most common cause of decline.

common_name: Millstream Daphne Moss Phlox (Compact Hot-Pink Creeping Phlox)

planting.note: Plant in well-drained to dry, lean, neutral to slightly alkaline soil in full sun; Millstream Daphne forms an especially tight, rounded clump, so give it slightly closer spacing than looser-spreading moss phlox cultivars.

directions: Plant in well-drained to dry, lean, neutral to slightly alkaline soil in full sun. Millstream Daphne, bred at Millstream Gardens, forms a short, tight, rounded cushion of needle-like evergreen foliage that disappears each spring beneath hot-pink flowers marked with a darker pink eye, giving more visual depth than solid-colored cultivars. Its compact, slow-spreading habit suits small rock garden pockets, trough plantings, and wall crevices where a looser, fast-spreading cultivar would overrun neighbors. Shear back lightly after the spring bloom to tidy the clump and can encourage a light rebloom, and keep the site sharply drained to avoid crown rot.

common_name: Fort Hill Moss Phlox (Rose-Pink Creeping Phlox)

planting.note: Plant in well-drained to dry, lean, neutral to slightly alkaline soil in full sun; Fort Hill tolerates hot, dry sites better than most creeping phlox cultivars, making it a good choice for exposed slopes and sandy banks.

directions: Plant in well-drained to dry, lean, neutral to slightly alkaline soil in full sun. Fort Hill blankets its low, needle-like evergreen foliage each spring in fragrant, deeply notched lavender-pink flowers with a red-purple eye, a fragrant bicolor effect distinct from the solid tones of 'Emerald Pink' or 'Scarlet Flame'. The dense, mat-forming habit thrives in sandy or gravelly soil and holds up to hot, dry conditions better than many other moss phlox selections, making it well suited to sunbaked slopes and rock walls. Shear lightly after bloom to keep growth tight and compact, and avoid heavy or wet soils, which quickly lead to thinning and crown rot.

common_name: Sammy Russell Daylily (Classic Reblooming Red)

planting.note: Plant divisions in spring in average, well-drained soil in full sun; established clumps rebloom reliably and need dividing only every four to five years.

directions: Registered in the early 1950s and named for pioneering hybridizer Sammy Russell, this small-flowered orange-red diploid was among the first daylilies widely recognized for dependable rebloom in northern gardens rather than a single midsummer flush. Sturdy, well-branched scapes carry a long succession of modestly sized blooms over many weeks, making a single well-grown clump far more productive than its flower size suggests. It thrives in ordinary garden soil with average moisture and shrugs off both cold winters and hot summers with minimal care. Divide congested clumps in spring or after flowering to keep bloom count high and refresh the planting.

common_name: Tetrina's Daughter Daylily (Award-Winning Yellow Spider)

planting.note: Plant divisions in spring in fertile, well-drained soil in full sun; give room for the narrow-petaled scapes to arch without crowding neighboring perennials.

directions: Introduced in the late 1970s, Tetrina's Daughter helped popularize the narrow-petaled spider form among mainstream gardeners with its clear, unpatterned lemon-yellow flowers and graceful, elongated segments. Tall, well-branched scapes hold the blooms above the clean grassy foliage, giving the clump a light, airy look distinct from the rounder-flowered cultivars that dominated earlier breeding. It performs reliably across a wide range of climates and multiplies at a moderate pace without becoming aggressive. Grow in full sun and average garden soil, dividing every three to four years to maintain vigorous flowering.

common_name: Siloam Peony Display Daylily (Double Pink Siloam Series)

planting.note: Plant divisions in spring in fertile, well-drained soil in full sun; the fully double blooms show best where scapes are sheltered from heavy afternoon storms.

directions: Bred by Arkansas hybridizer Pauline Henry as part of her renowned Siloam series, this cultivar produces fully double, ruffled pink flowers with a rose-red eye and green throat that closely resemble small peony blossoms rather than a typical single-form daylily. The compact clump stays tidy and floriferous, making it a popular choice for smaller borders and mixed perennial beds where its unusual flower form draws attention. Grow in full sun for the heaviest bud count, though it tolerates a bit of afternoon shade in hotter regions. Divide every three to four years once the clump becomes crowded to keep the doubling consistent.

common_name: Crystal Blue Persuasion Daylily (Lavender Reblooming Diploid)

planting.note: Plant divisions in spring in well-drained soil in full sun; consistent moisture through the growing season supports its extended rebloom cycles.

directions: Hybridized by Grace Stamile and named for the 1960s pop song, this diploid daylily bears fragrant, lavender-blue flowers accented by a deeper purple eyezone and a chartreuse-green throat. It is valued for extra-early and extra-late rebloom cycles that stretch its flowering season well beyond a single midsummer flush in favorable climates. Compact, well-branched scapes hold the ruffled blooms just above tidy, disease-resistant foliage. Grow in full sun with regular moisture and divide every three to four years to sustain the heaviest repeat bloom.

common_name: Frankly Scarlet Daylily (Rainbow Rhythm Series Red Rebloomer)

planting.note: Plant divisions in spring in well-drained soil in full sun; part of Darrel Apps's Rainbow Rhythm breeding line selected for heavy repeat bloom on compact plants.

directions: Part of hybridizer Darrel Apps's Rainbow Rhythm series bred for garden performance, Frankly Scarlet produces vivid true-red flowers with a small green throat on compact, well-branched scapes that stand cleanly above the foliage. The series was developed to rebloom heavily over a long season rather than produce one large flush, and this cultivar is one of its most widely planted red-flowered members. It holds up well in heat and humidity and resists common daylily foliage issues better than many older reds. Grow in full sun in average garden soil and divide congested clumps every three to four years.

common_name: Going Bananas Daylily (Rainbow Rhythm Series Reblooming Yellow)

planting.note: Plant divisions in spring in well-drained soil in full sun; this Rainbow Rhythm series selection reblooms continuously from early summer into fall with deadheading of spent scapes.

directions: Bred by Darrel Apps as part of the Rainbow Rhythm series, Going Bananas bears clear, unmarked lemon-yellow flowers over a remarkably long season, often continuing to open new blooms from early summer clear into fall in favorable climates. Its compact, tidy habit and near-constant flowering have made it one of the most commercially popular reblooming daylilies of the past two decades. The plant stays vigorous without becoming invasive, forming a dense but manageable clump. Grow in full sun in average, well-drained soil and divide every three to four years once flowering begins to decline.

common_name: Chase the Sun Daylily (Rainbow Rhythm Series Apricot Rebloomer)

planting.note: Plant divisions in spring in well-drained soil in full sun; consistent moisture during summer supports the long rebloom cycle typical of this Rainbow Rhythm selection.

directions: Another Darrel Apps introduction in the Rainbow Rhythm series, Chase the Sun carries warm apricot-orange flowers with a lightly ruffled edge on tall, well-branched scapes that rise cleanly above the foliage clump. Bred specifically for extended garden performance, it produces new bloom scapes in continuous waves through summer rather than a single concentrated flush. The clump stays vigorous and disease-resistant in a range of climates, from humid Southern gardens to cold-winter regions. Grow in full sun in average, well-drained soil and divide every three to four years to maintain peak flowering.

common_name: Sultan's Palace Bearded Iris (Velvety Maroon-Red Self Iris)

planting.note: Plant rhizomes in late summer to early fall so the fans establish before frost; Sultan's Palace carries deep, velvety maroon-red color that intensifies in full sun.

directions: Set rhizomes shallowly with the top exposed to direct sun in sharply drained soil, as excess moisture around the rhizome invites rot far more readily than dry spells harm this iris. Hybridized by Robert Schreiner in 1977 from a Glowing Tiara x Spartan cross and introduced in 1981, Sultan's Palace is named for its rich, brooding color: heavy maroon-red velvet falls beneath slightly ruffled standards of the same tailored self tone, with a self-colored beard. Divide crowded clumps every three to four years after bloom, discarding the spent center rhizomes and resetting vigorous outer fans.

common_name: Yaquina Blue Bearded Iris (Dykes Medal-Winning Ruffled Blue Iris)

planting.note: Plant rhizomes in late summer to early fall with tops exposed to sun; Yaquina Blue is a Dykes Medal winner prized for its clean medium-blue ruffled blooms.

directions: Plant rhizomes horizontally with the top surface exposed to sunlight in well-drained soil, since standing moisture causes rot more readily than this iris is troubled by drought. Introduced by Schreiner's Gardens in 1992, Yaquina Blue won the American Iris Society's Dykes Medal in 2001 for its showy, heavily ruffled medium-blue flowers with a yellow beard tipped white, carried on strong branching stems. It has also become an influential parent, siring dozens of later blue-toned introductions. Divide every three to four years after bloom to keep clumps vigorous and floriferous.

common_name: Honky Tonk Blues Bearded Iris (Dykes Medal-Winning Streaked Blue Iris)

planting.note: Plant rhizomes in late summer to early fall with tops exposed to sun; Honky Tonk Blues is a Dykes Medal winner known for its ruffled blue blooms with fine white-grey streaking.

directions: Set rhizomes shallowly with the top exposed to full sun in sharply drained soil to avoid rot. Hybridized by Schreiner's Gardens from a 1988 cross and awarded the Dykes Medal in 1995, Honky Tonk Blues bears ruffled blue flowers delicately streaked and edged in white-grey on the falls, with hyacinth-blue beards, held on extra-strong, well-branched stems with up to ten buds per stalk. Its vigor and heavy bud count make it a long-blooming garden standout. Lift and divide congested clumps every three to four years after flowering finishes.

common_name: Mesmerizer Bearded Iris (Dykes Medal-Winning Reblooming White Iris)

planting.note: Plant rhizomes in late summer to early fall so fans root in before frost; Mesmerizer is a Dykes Medal-winning white iris that often reblooms in fall in mild climates.

directions: Set rhizomes with the tops exposed to sun in well-drained soil, since wet feet cause rot more readily than this iris minds a dry spell. Hybridized by Monty Byers and registered in 1990, Mesmerizer earned the American Iris Society's Dykes Medal in 2002 for its dramatically ruffled white flowers, each falls flounce accented by a tangerine-red beard and finished with a pale green button at the center. It blooms in midseason and reblooms in many gardens with a second flush later in the year. Divide crowded clumps every three to four years after bloom for continued vigor.

common_name: Total Recall Bearded Iris (Reblooming White-and-Yellow Iris)

planting.note: Plant rhizomes in late summer to early fall with the tops exposed to sun; Total Recall is a dependable rebloomer reported to flower again in fall across a wide range of zones.

directions: Plant rhizomes shallowly with tops exposed to full sun in sharply drained soil, as soggy ground causes rot faster than drought causes harm. Registered by Ben Hager in 1992, Total Recall bears ruffled flowers with light-to-medium yellow standards over white falls edged in yellow and a light yellow beard, opening from early into late season. It is one of the most widely reported rebloomers in the trade, with fall rebloom documented across dozens of states and zones 4 through 10. Divide congested clumps every three to four years after the main bloom to sustain rebloom performance.

common_name: Starwoman Intermediate Bearded Iris (Dykes Medal-Winning Purple-and-Pearl Iris)

planting.note: Plant rhizomes in late summer to early fall with the tops exposed to sun; Starwoman is the only Intermediate Bearded iris ever to win the Dykes Medal.

directions: Set rhizomes shallowly with tops exposed to sun in well-drained soil to prevent rot. Bred from 'Chubby Cheeks' crossed with a Keppel seedling and introduced by Aitken in 1998, Starwoman carries blackish royal-purple standards over pearl-ground falls rimmed and striped in dark violet, with blue-violet beards tipped gold. It won the American Iris Society's Dykes Medal in 2008, a rare honor for the smaller-statured Intermediate Bearded class. Divide clumps every two to three years after bloom, since Intermediate Beardeds tend to multiply and crowd faster than Tall Beardeds.

common_name: Gypsy Romance Bearded Iris (Ruffled Violet-Raspberry Iris)

planting.note: Plant rhizomes in late summer to early fall with tops exposed to sun; Gypsy Romance is a Wister Medal winner valued for its rich violet-raspberry ruffled blooms.

directions: Set rhizomes horizontally with the top exposed to sun in sharply drained soil, since wet conditions cause rot far more readily than this iris minds drought. Introduced by Schreiner's Gardens in 1994, Gypsy Romance carries heavily ruffled, rich violet-raspberry standards and falls with vivid blue-purple beards, opening in a well-spaced candelabra of bloom during late midseason. It won the American Iris Society's Wister Medal in 2002 for garden performance, and is notably drought-tolerant and deer-resistant once established. Divide crowded clumps every three to four years after flowering to maintain vigor.

common_name: Splashacata Bearded Iris (Dykes Medal-Winning Speckled Broken-Color Iris)

planting.note: Plant rhizomes in late summer to early fall with tops exposed to sun; Splashacata is a Dykes Medal winner known for its unusual purple-speckled falls.

directions: Plant rhizomes shallowly with the top exposed to full sun in well-drained soil to avoid rhizome rot. Hybridized by Richard Tasco and introduced in 1998, Splashacata displays pale lavender-violet standards over white falls heavily peppered with purple dots and speckles, an eye-catching 'broken color' pattern rare among bearded iris. It won the American Iris Society's Dykes Medal in 2005 after a run of lesser awards, and remains a favorite for its novelty coloring on a vigorous, well-branched plant. Divide congested clumps every three to four years after bloom.

common_name: Dividing Line Miniature Tall Bearded Iris (Dykes Medal-Winning Pale Violet Iris)

planting.note: Plant rhizomes in late summer to early fall with tops exposed to sun; Dividing Line is the only Miniature Tall Bearded iris ever to win the Dykes Medal.

directions: Set rhizomes shallowly with the top exposed to sun in well-drained soil, since this smaller-statured class is just as prone to rot in soggy ground as full-size Tall Beardeds. Hybridized by Charles Bunnell and registered in 2004, Dividing Line carries pale blue-violet standards fading to blue-white above pale purple falls marked with a darker violet spot and yellow beards, on slender stems suited to the Miniature Tall Bearded class's proportionate, narrow-petaled form. It won the American Iris Society's Dykes Medal in 2014, a first for its class. Divide every two to three years after bloom to keep the clump from crowding itself out.

common_name: Wearing Rubies Bearded Iris (Reblooming Rose-and-Ruby Iris)

planting.note: Plant rhizomes in late summer to early fall with tops exposed to sun; Wearing Rubies has ruby-red falls and a musky fragrance, and reblooms in mild-winter gardens.

directions: Set rhizomes horizontally with the top exposed to sun in sharply drained soil to prevent rot. Bred by Australian hybridizer Barry Blyth and registered in 2000, Wearing Rubies pairs rose-toned, ruffled standards with deep ruby-red falls and a golden beard highlight, opening early in the season with a musky fragrance. Rebloom has been reported in warmer climates such as California, Oregon, and Australia, making it a good pick for zones 8 and 9 gardeners chasing a fall encore. Divide crowded clumps every three to four years after bloom to keep flowering strong.

common_name: Bride's Halo Bearded Iris (Dykes Medal-Winning White-and-Gold Iris)

planting.note: Plant rhizomes in late summer to early fall with tops exposed to sun; Bride's Halo is a Dykes Medal winner with ruffled white blooms edged in gold.

directions: Plant rhizomes shallowly with the top exposed to full sun in well-drained soil, since standing moisture invites rot more readily than this iris is troubled by dry spells. Hybridized by Hubert C. Mohr from a Rainbow Gold x Denver Mint cross and registered in 1971, Bride's Halo bears heavily ruffled and lightly laced white flowers finished with a narrow yellow band at the edge and a yellow beard. It won the American Iris Society's Dykes Medal in 1978 and remains valued for its drought and deer resistance. Divide congested clumps every three to four years after bloom to maintain vigor.

common_name: Feed Back Bearded Iris (Fragrant Reblooming Violet Iris)

planting.note: Plant rhizomes in late summer to early fall with tops exposed to sun; Feed Back is a widely reported rebloomer with fragrant mid-violet flowers.

directions: Set rhizomes horizontally with the top exposed to sun in sharply drained soil to prevent rhizome rot. Registered by Ben Hager in 1983 from a Cloud Baron x Perfume Counter cross, Feed Back produces sweetly fragrant, mid-violet flowers with yellow beards from early into midseason, then reliably sends up a second flush in early autumn across a very wide range of climates. Its rebloom has been documented from the Gulf Coast to the upper Midwest and into Canada. Divide crowded clumps every three to four years after the main bloom to keep both bloom cycles strong.
